subject: math
title: Exponents, Roots, and Scientific Notation
objectives: You will evaluate powers with positive, zero, and negative exponents, including powers of negative numbers.
You will use the product, quotient, and power rules to simplify expressions with exponents.
You will find square roots and cube roots, estimate roots that are not whole numbers, and simplify square roots.
You will convert between standard form and scientific notation, compare numbers in scientific notation, and multiply and divide them in real-world problems.
You will evaluate expressions that combine exponents, roots, and grouping symbols using the order of operations.

slides.title: Week 3 Math: Exponents, Roots, and Scientific Notation
slides.board:
Exponents, Roots, and Scientific Notation

  • Evaluate powers, including zero and negative exponents
  • Simplify with the product, quotient, and power rules
  • Find, estimate, and simplify square roots and cube roots
  • Read, write, compare, and compute in scientific notation
  • Use the order of operations with exponents and roots

Today: warm-up, exponents, exponent rules, roots, scientific notation, order of operations, GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 3. Today we learn the shorthand for repeated multiplication, how to undo it with roots, and how scientists write enormous and tiny numbers without a page full of zeros. These skills show up all over the GED, and many of them appear on the first part of the math test, where you cannot use a calculator. Same plan as always: I explain a rule, show you a worked example, we do some together, and then you try some on your own while I watch the clock.
ask: What do you think 2<sup>3</sup> means? (expected answer: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8; if the student says 6, note it, because slide 3 fixes exactly that)
notes.watch: Pacing for 60 minutes: warm-up 5 min (slide 2); exponents and exponent rules 17 min (slides 3–11); roots 10 min (slides 12–15); scientific notation 14 min (slides 16–21); order of operations 9 min (slides 22–25); strategy and recap 5 min (slides 26–27). If you fall behind, cut each we-do slide to two problems and skip the fourth problem on the you-do slides.

slides.title: Warm-up: Week 2 Review
slides.board:
Last week: ratios, rates, proportions, and percents. No calculator.

  1. Simplify the ratio 18 : 24.
  2. 6 notebooks cost $9. What is the price per notebook?
  3. Solve 3/5 = x/20.
  4. What is 15% of 80?
  5. A $40 shirt is 25% off. What is the sale price?
steps: 1. The GCF of 18 and 24 is 6: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4, so 3 : 4.
2. Unit price = cost ÷ units = $9 ÷ 6 = $1.50 per notebook.
4. 10% of 80 is 8 and 5% is 4, so 15% is 8 + 4 = 12. (Or 0.15 × 80 = 12.)
5. 25% of $40 is $10, so the sale price is $40 − $10 = $30. (Or $40 × 0.75 = $30.)

notes.say: Let's warm up with last week's skills, because they come back in every unit from here on. Take about three minutes and work all five on paper, then tell me your answers one at a time. Notice how often we multiply and divide by 10 and 100 in these problems: today we turn powers of 10 into a tool of their own.
ask: How did you find 15% of 80 without a calculator? (expected answer: 10% is 8, 5% is half of that, 4; 8 + 4 = 12)
On number 5, what is the quickest way to get the sale price in one step? (expected answer: multiply by 0.75, because you pay 75%)
notes.watch: If number 5 comes back as $10, the student found the discount and stopped; ask "Is that what you pay, or what you save?" If number 3 comes back as 33 1/3, the cross products were set up wrong (3x = 5 × 20); have them write 3 × 20 and 5 × x side by side. Keep this to five minutes; the rest of today is new material.

slides.title: What an Exponent Means
slides.board:
53 = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125   (base 5, exponent 3)   Not 5 × 3.

Power2122232425
Value2481632
  • 10n = 1 followed by n zeros: 104 = 10,000
  • The exponent touches only what is right next to it:
    (−3)2 = (−3)(−3) = 9   but   −32 = −(3 × 3) = −9

notes.say: An exponent is a counter. It tells you how many times to use the base as a factor. So 5 to the third is three fives multiplied together, 125, and never 5 times 3. We read 5 squared for the second power and 5 cubed for the third. Powers of 10 are the friendliest: the exponent is the number of zeros. The trickiest part is a negative base. The exponent only grabs what it touches. With parentheses, the negative sign is part of the base; without them, the exponent touches only the number and the negative sign waits until the end.
ask: What is 4<sup>3</sup>? (expected answer: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64)
What is 10<sup>6</sup>? (expected answer: 1,000,000, one million)
Which is negative, (−4)<sup>2</sup> or −4<sup>2</sup>? (expected answer: −4<sup>2</sup> = −16; (−4)<sup>2</sup> = 16)
notes.watch: The number one exponent error is base times exponent (4<sup>3</sup> = 12). Until it is automatic, have the student write out the repeated multiplication every time. For negative bases, ask "What does the exponent touch?" and have them circle the base.

slides.title: Powers and Negative Bases
slides.board:
Evaluate each expression.

(a) 25    (b) (−3)4    (c) −34    (d) (−2)3

Method: find the base, write the repeated multiplication, then multiply two factors at a time.
steps: (b) The base is −3: (−3)(−3)(−3)(−3) = 9 × 9 = 81. Four negative factors, an even number, so positive.
(d) The base is −2: (−2)(−2)(−2) = 4 × (−2) = −8. Three negative factors, an odd number, so negative.

notes.say: Watch how I find the base first in every problem. In (b), the parentheses put the negative sign inside the base, so it gets multiplied four times. In (c), there are no parentheses, so I raise 3 to the fourth and put the negative sign on at the end. Part (d) uses the Week 1 sign rule: count the negative factors. An even count gives a positive answer; an odd count gives a negative answer.
ask: Why are (b) and (c) different? (expected answer: in (b) the negative is inside the parentheses, so it is part of the base; in (c) the exponent touches only the 3)
Without multiplying, is (−1)<sup>9</sup> positive or negative? (expected answer: negative; nine negative factors is odd)
notes.watch: If the student gets 81 for (c), point at the base: "Is the negative sign inside the parentheses?" If they get 8 for (d), they lost track of the third negative factor; have them write all three factors.

slides.title: Product, Quotient, and Power Rules
slides.board:
These rules work only when the bases are the same.

RuleDo thisExample
xa · xb = xa+bMultiplying: add exponentsx2 · x3 = x5
xa ÷ xb = xa−bDividing: subtract exponentsx7 ÷ x2 = x5
(xa)b = xabPower of a power: multiply(x2)3 = x6
(xy)a = xayaPower of a product: every factor(2x)3 = 8x3

notes.say: Every rule here comes straight from the meaning of an exponent, so you can rebuild any of them on test day. x squared times x cubed is two x's times three more x's: five x's, so we add. x to the seventh over x squared: two x's on the bottom cancel two on top, leaving five, so we subtract. And x squared, cubed, is x squared written three times, which is six x's, so we multiply. Numbers in front, the coefficients, are ordinary numbers: you multiply or divide them as usual. None of these rules work with different bases, or with addition.
ask: Write x<sup>2</sup> · x<sup>3</sup> the long way. How many x's? (expected answer: x · x · x · x · x, five, so x<sup>5</sup>)
Can you combine 2<sup>3</sup> · 3<sup>2</sup> into one power? (expected answer: no, the bases are different; evaluate instead: 8 × 9 = 72)
notes.watch: The classic mix-up is multiplying exponents in x<sup>2</sup> · x<sup>3</sup> (getting x<sup>6</sup>) or adding them in (x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>3</sup> (getting x<sup>5</sup>). When it happens, write both the long way side by side. Also watch for 2<sup>3</sup> + 2<sup>2</sup> = 2<sup>5</sup>: the rules never apply to addition (8 + 4 = 12, not 32).

slides.title: Using the Rules Together
slides.board:
Simplify:   (2x3)2 · x4 ÷ x5

Method: powers of products first, then multiply, then divide. Handle numbers and variables separately.
steps: Power of a product, every factor: (2x<sup>3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 2<sup>2</sup> · x<sup>3×2</sup> = 4x<sup>6</sup>
Check with x = 2: (2 · 8)<sup>2</sup> · 16 ÷ 32 = 256 · 16 ÷ 32 = 128, and 4 · 2<sup>5</sup> = 4 · 32 = 128. It matches.

notes.say: When several rules meet in one problem, go in order and write one line per rule. The power outside the parentheses goes to every factor inside, including the 2. That is the step people skip. Then I combine the x's with the product rule and finish with the quotient rule. The last line is a habit I want you to build: plug in a small number like 2 to check. If both sides give the same value, the simplification is right.
ask: What is the most common wrong answer here? (expected answer: 2x<sup>5</sup>, from forgetting to square the 2)
Why check with x = 2 instead of x = 1? (expected answer: every power of 1 is 1, so x = 1 cannot catch an exponent mistake)
notes.watch: If the student writes (2x<sup>3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 2x<sup>6</sup> or 4x<sup>5</sup>, slow down and write (2x<sup>3</sup>)(2x<sup>3</sup>) the long way: 2 · 2 = 4 and x<sup>3</sup> · x<sup>3</sup> = x<sup>6</sup>.

slides.title: Zero and Negative Exponents
slides.board:
Follow the pattern: each step down divides by 2.

232221202−12−22−3
84211/21/41/8
  • x0 = 1 for any x ≠ 0.   70 = 1
  • x−n = 1/xn: a negative exponent means reciprocal, not a negative number.   2−3 = 1/8
  • Powers of 10: 10−1 = 0.1,   10−2 = 0.01,   10−3 = 0.001

notes.say: Here is where people start guessing, so let's use a pattern instead. Going down the powers of 2, each step divides by 2: 8, 4, 2. One more step gives 2 divided by 2, which is 1, so 2 to the zero is 1. Keep going: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8. That is why a negative exponent means reciprocal. The answer stays positive; it just gets small. You can also see the zero rule from the quotient rule: x to the fourth over x to the fourth is x to the zero, and anything divided by itself is 1.
ask: What is 9<sup>0</sup>? (expected answer: 1)
What is 3<sup>−2</sup>? (expected answer: 1/3<sup>2</sup> = 1/9)
Is 5<sup>−2</sup> a negative number? (expected answer: no; it is 1/25, a small positive number)
notes.watch: Expect 2<sup>−3</sup> = −8 or −6, and 7<sup>0</sup> = 0. Send the student back to the pattern table every time; do not just restate the rule.

slides.title: Zero and Negative Exponents at Work
slides.board: (a) 5−2    (b) 10−3 as a decimal    (c) 40 + 4−1    (d) Simplify x3 · x−5

notes.say: Each of these is one rule applied carefully. In (a), the negative exponent flips 5 squared into the denominator. In (b), notice that 10 to the negative 3 has the 1 in the third decimal place; that fact powers scientific notation later today. In (c), the zero power is 1, not 0. And (d) shows the product rule still works with negative exponents: 3 plus negative 5 is negative 2, and we usually rewrite the answer with a positive exponent.
ask: In (c), what answer do you get if you think 4<sup>0</sup> = 0? (expected answer: 1/4, which is wrong)
How many zeros are between the decimal point and the 1 in 10<sup>−3</sup> = 0.001? (expected answer: two; the 1 is in the third place)
notes.watch: On (d), students sometimes multiply 3 × (−5) = −15. Ask: "Are we multiplying powers, or raising a power to a power?" Multiplying powers adds the exponents.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Equivalent Expressions
slides.board:
Which expression is equivalent to

(3x2)3 ÷ (9x4)?

A. x2    B. 3x    C. 3x2    D. 3x10
steps: Eliminate A (x2): it comes from writing 33 as 3 × 3 = 9, so 9x6 ÷ 9x4 = x2. But 33 = 27.
Eliminate B (3x): it comes from adding exponents in the power: (x2)3 written as x5, so 27x5 ÷ 9x4 = 3x. A power of a power multiplies: x6.
Eliminate D (3x10): it comes from adding the exponents when dividing (6 + 4). Dividing powers subtracts: 6 − 4 = 2.
C (3x2) is correct: (3x2)3 = 27x6; 27 ÷ 9 = 3 and x6 ÷ x4 = x2.

notes.say: "Which expression is equivalent" is one of the most common GED wordings for exponent rules. Each wrong choice is built from one specific slip. Work it yourself first, one rule per line, and then use the wrong choices as a checklist of traps you avoided. If you are ever unsure, plug in x = 2: the original gives 1,728 ÷ 144 = 12, and of the four choices only 3x<sup>2</sup> also gives 12.
ask: Which choice did you get, and what was your first line? (expected answer: C, 3x<sup>2</sup>; first line (3x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>3</sup> = 27x<sup>6</sup>)
notes.answer: C (3x<sup>2</sup>). (3x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>3</sup> = 3<sup>3</sup>x<sup>6</sup> = 27x<sup>6</sup>; 27x<sup>6</sup> ÷ 9x<sup>4</sup> = 3x<sup>2</sup>. Plug-in check with x = 2: (3 · 4)<sup>3</sup> ÷ (9 · 16) = 1,728 ÷ 144 = 12, and 3 · 2<sup>2</sup> = 12.
notes.watch: If the student picked A, B, or D, read the matching elimination step and have them find the exact line where their work left the correct path. A is the most common trap: the student cubes the variable part but squares, or doubles, the 3 instead of cubing it.

slides.title: Square Roots and Cube Roots
slides.board:
√49 = 7 because 72 = 49.   ∛125 = 5 because 53 = 125.   ∛(−8) = −2.

n456789101112
n2162536496481100121144
  • Estimate: 36 < 40 < 49, so 6 < √40 < 7
  • Simplify: pull out the largest perfect square. √50 = √(25 × 2) = 5√2
  • √(a + b) ≠ √a + √b:   √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5, not 7

notes.say: A root undoes a power. The square root asks, "What number times itself gives this?" and the cube root asks, "What number used three times gives this?" On the GED, the square root symbol means the positive root. A cube root of a negative number is fine, because a negative times a negative times a negative is negative. The square root of a negative number is not a real number. When a number is not a perfect square, trap it between two perfect squares to estimate. To simplify, split off the largest perfect-square factor. And remember the root bar is a grouping symbol: add underneath it first.
ask: What is √81? ∛27? (expected answer: 9 and 3)
√70 is between which two whole numbers? (expected answer: 8 and 9, because 64 < 70 < 81)
Why does ∛(−64) work but √(−64) does not? (expected answer: (−4)<sup>3</sup> = −64, but no real number squared is negative)
notes.watch: Students often halve the number for a square root (√64 = 32) or divide by 3 for a cube root (∛27 = 9). Ask the "undo" question: "What times itself gives 64?" Insist on knowing the perfect squares through 15<sup>2</sup> = 225 and the cubes through 5<sup>3</sup> = 125 by heart; the no-calculator part depends on it.

slides.title: Cube Roots, Estimates, and Simplifying
slides.board:
(a) ∛(−125)    (b) Estimate √55    (c) Simplify √48

Method: test a number for the cube root; trap the estimate between two perfect squares; pull out the largest perfect-square factor.
steps: (b, continued) 55 is 6 away from 49 and 9 away from 64, so √55 is closer to 7: about 7.4 (a calculator gives 7.416…).
(c) Perfect-square factors of 48: 4 and 16. Use the largest, 16: √48 = √(16 × 3) = √16 × √3 = 4√3

notes.say: Three different root skills. For the cube root, I test a number and multiply it three times; the sign carries through. For the estimate, I trap 55 between the perfect squares 49 and 64 and notice it is closer to 49. For simplifying, I list perfect squares that divide 48 and choose the biggest. If you choose a smaller one, like 4, you get 2√12, which is equal but not finished, because 12 still has a perfect-square factor.
ask: If you pulled out 4 instead of 16 in (c), what would you get, and is it finished? (expected answer: 2√12; not finished, since 12 = 4 × 3, so it becomes 4√3)
notes.watch: On (c), the common error is 16√3: the student pulled 16 out without taking its root. Have them check by squaring: (16√3)<sup>2</sup> = 768, not 48.

slides.title: Scientific Notation
slides.board:
a × 10n, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer.

Standard formScientific notation
93,000,000 miles (Earth to Sun)9.3 × 107
0.000002 meter (a bacterium)2 × 10−6
  1. Move the decimal point until exactly one nonzero digit is to its left.
  2. Count the moves: that is the size of the exponent.
  3. Number 10 or more: positive exponent. Number less than 1: negative exponent.

notes.say: Scientists, engineers, and budget reports all need to write huge and tiny numbers, and scientific notation does it with a front number between 1 and 10 times a power of 10. The front number keeps the important digits; the exponent tells where the decimal point really belongs. To convert, slide the decimal point until there is one nonzero digit in front of it, count the moves, and decide the sign: big numbers get positive exponents, numbers smaller than 1 get negative exponents. Going back to standard form, you move the point the other way.
ask: Is 45 × 10<sup>3</sup> in scientific notation? Why or why not? (expected answer: no; 45 is not less than 10; it should be 4.5 × 10<sup>4</sup>)
Will 0.0008 have a positive or a negative exponent? (expected answer: negative, because it is less than 1)
notes.watch: The most common error is the sign of the exponent. Ask one question every time: "Is the number bigger than 10 or smaller than 1?" Then check by moving the decimal back.

slides.title: Converting Both Ways
slides.board:
(a) Write 384,000 km (Earth to Moon) in scientific notation.
(b) Write 0.0000075 m (a red blood cell) in scientific notation.
(c) Write 2.06 × 104 in standard form.
(d) Fix 25 × 103 so it is in scientific notation.
steps: (a) 384,000 → 3.84000: the point moved 5 places left. Big number, positive exponent: 3.84 × 105 km
(b) 0.0000075 → 7.5: the point moved 6 places right. Less than 1, negative exponent: 7.5 × 10−6 m
(c) Positive exponent 4: move the point 4 places right, filling with zeros: 2.06 → 20,600

notes.say: Watch me count every move out loud. In (a), I move left five places, and since the number is large the exponent is positive 5. In (b), I move right six places to get past all those zeros, and since the number is tiny the exponent is negative 6. In (c), the exponent tells me to move right four places, and I fill empty places with zeros. In (d), the front number is too big, so I rewrite it and use the product rule on the powers of 10.
ask: In (c), why is the answer not 2,060,000? (expected answer: that adds four zeros to 206; you move the decimal point four places, which gives 20,600)
In (d), the front number got smaller. What happened to the exponent? (expected answer: it went up by 1, from 3 to 4)
notes.watch: Watch for counting errors in (b): students often count the zeros (5) instead of the moves (6). Have them draw a hop for each place the point moves.

slides.title: Computing and Comparing in Scientific Notation
slides.board:
• Multiply: multiply the fronts, add the exponents.
    (3 × 104)(5 × 106) = 15 × 1010 = 1.5 × 1011
  • Divide: divide the fronts, subtract the exponents.
    (8 × 109) ÷ (4 × 106) = 2 × 103
  • Adjust: front bigger than 10: divide it by 10, add 1 to the exponent. Front less than 1: multiply by 10, subtract 1.
  • Compare: exponents first; if they match, compare the fronts. 2 × 105 > 9 × 104

notes.say: Computing in scientific notation is just this week's exponent rules with a base of 10. Multiply the front numbers and add the exponents; divide the front numbers and subtract the exponents. Then look at the front number. If it is 10 or more, or less than 1, adjust it and balance the change in the exponent. To compare, look at the exponents first, because each step in the exponent is a factor of ten, which outweighs any difference in the front numbers.
ask: Which is greater, 9 × 10<sup>4</sup> or 2 × 10<sup>5</sup>? (expected answer: 2 × 10<sup>5</sup> = 200,000, which is more than 90,000)
Adjust 0.6 × 10<sup>8</sup>. (expected answer: 6 × 10<sup>7</sup>)
notes.watch: Students adjust in the wrong direction: 15 × 10<sup>10</sup> becomes 1.5 × 10<sup>9</sup>. Teach the balance idea: if the front number gets 10 times smaller, the power of 10 must get 10 times bigger.

slides.title: A Division Word Problem
slides.board: A hard drive holds about 2 × 1012 bytes. One photo uses about 4 × 106 bytes. About how many photos fit on the drive?
steps: How many photos fit means total ÷ size of one: (2 × 10<sup>12</sup>) ÷ (4 × 10<sup>6</sup>)
Divide the fronts: 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5. Subtract the exponents: 12 − 6 = 6. So far: 0.5 × 10<sup>6</sup>
Adjust: 0.5 is less than 1, so 0.5 = 5 × 10−1, and 5 × 10−1 × 106 = 5 × 105
In standard form: 500,000 photos. Sense check: 500,000 × 4,000,000 = 2,000,000,000,000. It matches.

notes.say: The words "how many fit" or "how many times greater" mean divide. I divide the front numbers and subtract the exponents. The front number comes out to 0.5, which is not between 1 and 10, so I adjust: multiplying the front by 10 means taking one away from the exponent. Last, I check by multiplying back.
ask: What answer do you get if you change 0.5 to 5 but leave the exponent at 6? (expected answer: 5 × 10<sup>6</sup>, which is ten times too big)
What operation would you use to find the total bytes for 300 photos? (expected answer: multiply)
notes.watch: Two common traps: dividing in the wrong order (photo size ÷ drive size gives 2 × 10<sup>−6</sup>, a tiny number that makes no sense for a count) and forgetting to adjust the exponent.

  2. Write 3.1 × 10−3 in standard form.
  3. (2 × 105)(4.5 × 102)
  4. (6 × 108) ÷ (1.5 × 102)

notes.say: Three minutes on the clock. Write the plan for each problem in a few words next to it: "point left 7," "add exponents," and so on. Then read me your answers.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: 5.2 × 10<sup>7</sup>; 0.0031; 9 × 10<sup>7</sup>; 4 × 10<sup>6</sup>)
notes.answer: (1) the point moves 7 places left: 5.2 × 10<sup>7</sup>   (2) move 3 places left: 0.0031   (3) 2 × 4.5 = 9 and 5 + 2 = 7: 9 × 10<sup>7</sup>   (4) 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4 and 8 − 2 = 6: 4 × 10<sup>6</sup>
notes.watch: 5.2 × 10<sup>6</sup> on number 1 means the student counted the zeros (6) instead of the moves (7). 3,100 on number 2 means the point moved the wrong way. 4 × 10<sup>10</sup> on number 4 means the exponents were added.

slides.title: Order of Operations with Exponents and Roots
slides.board:
1. Grouping: ( ), [ ], | |, a fraction bar, and everything under a root
  2. Exponents and roots
  3. Multiply and divide, left to right
  4. Add and subtract, left to right

20 − 2 × 32  →  20 − 2 × 9  →  20 − 18 = 2   (not (20 − 2 × 3)2, not 62)

notes.say: This is the Week 1 order with exponents and roots added in their proper place, right after grouping. An exponent belongs only to the number or the parentheses right before it, so 2 times 3 squared means square the 3 first, then multiply by 2. The root bar is also a grouping symbol: everything under it gets simplified before you take the root. Rewrite the whole expression after every step, so nothing gets lost.
ask: In 2 × 3<sup>2</sup>, what gets squared? (expected answer: only the 3; 2 × 9 = 18)
What do you do first in √(9 + 16) − 2? (expected answer: add under the root: √25 = 5, then 5 − 2 = 3)
notes.watch: The habit to break is multiplying before squaring: 2 × 3<sup>2</sup> = 6<sup>2</sup> = 36. Ask "What does the exponent touch?" just as you did with negative bases.

slides.title: A Full Order-of-Operations Problem
slides.board:
Evaluate:   4 + 3(23 − 5)2 ÷ 9 − √16

Method: grouping, then exponents and roots, then × and ÷ left to right, then + and − left to right. Rewrite the expression after every step.
steps: Inside the parentheses, exponent first: 2<sup>3</sup> = 8, then 8 − 5 = 3. Now: 4 + 3(3)<sup>2</sup> ÷ 9 − √16
Multiply and divide, left to right: 3 × 9 = 27, then 27 ÷ 9 = 3. Now: 4 + 3 − 4
Add and subtract, left to right: 4 + 3 = 7, then 7 − 4 = 3

notes.say: I rewrite the whole expression after every step. Inside the parentheses there is an exponent, so even in there I do the power before the subtraction. Then I do all the exponents and roots at once, then multiplication and division from left to right, and finally addition and subtraction.
ask: What answer do you get if you multiply 3 × 3 before squaring? (expected answer: (9)<sup>2</sup> = 81, 81 ÷ 9 = 9, and 4 + 9 − 4 = 9, which is wrong)
notes.watch: Watch for students who compute 4 + 3 = 7 first and then multiply. Addition waits until the very end.

slides.title: Order of Operations Together
slides.board:
1. 20 − 2 × 32 + √25
  2. (1 + 2)2 × 2 − ∛8
  3. 62 ÷ 4 × 3
  4. −22 + (−3)2

notes.say: Together again. Before each step, tell me which level of the order you are on: grouping, exponents and roots, multiply and divide, or add and subtract. Number 4 brings back negative bases from the start of the lesson.
ask: On number 3, why not 4 × 3 first? (expected answer: multiplication and division are partners, done left to right, and the division comes first here)
On number 4, what does each exponent touch? (expected answer: the first touches only the 2; the second touches −3)

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Scientific Notation in Context
slides.board:
A healthy adult has about 5 × 106 red blood cells in each microliter of blood. A blood donation is about 4.5 × 105 microliters. About how many red blood cells are in one donation?

A. 2.25 × 1012    B. 2.25 × 1010    C. 9.5 × 1011    D. 1.1 × 101
steps: Eliminate D (1.1 × 101): it comes from dividing (5 ÷ 4.5 and 6 − 5). Cells per microliter times microliters gives total cells, so multiply. Also, 11 cells in a whole donation makes no sense.
Eliminate C (9.5 × 1011): it comes from adding the fronts (5 + 4.5). When you multiply numbers in scientific notation, multiply the fronts: 5 × 4.5 = 22.5.
Eliminate B (2.25 × 1010): it adjusts in the wrong direction. 22.5 × 1011: making the front 10 times smaller means making the exponent 1 bigger, not smaller.
A (2.25 × 1012) is correct: 5 × 4.5 = 22.5 and 6 + 5 = 11, so 22.5 × 1011 = 2.25 × 1012, about 2 trillion cells.

notes.say: This is how scientific notation shows up on the GED: inside a real-world context, often science or budgets. First decide the operation from the units: cells per microliter times microliters gives cells, so we multiply. Then multiply the fronts, add the exponents, and adjust. Then use the wrong choices as a checklist.
ask: Which choice did you get, and what operation did you use? (expected answer: A; multiply)
notes.watch: If the student picked B, practice the balance idea once more: 22.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> = 2.25 × 10 × 10<sup>11</sup> = 2.25 × 10<sup>12</sup>. If they picked D, have them say the units out loud: "cells per microliter times microliters."

slides.title: GED Strategy: Plug In a Number, and Know Your Calculator
slides.board:
1. Equivalent expressions: pick x = 2 (not 0 or 1), evaluate the original and each choice, and keep the one that matches.
  2. No calculator (Part 1): know perfect squares through 152 and cubes through 53.
  3. TI-30XS: x2 key for squares, ^ key for other powers, 2nd then x2 for √, and the ×10n key for scientific notation.
  4. Negative base: type the parentheses. (−3)2 = 9, but −32 = −9 on the calculator too.

notes.say: Two habits will save you points. First, when a question asks which expression is equivalent and you are unsure of a rule, plug in a small number like 2 and test the choices. Do not use 0 or 1, because every power of 1 is 1 and many choices will tie. Second, know your tools. The exponent rules are not on the GED formula sheet, so you need them in your head, and the first part of the test has no calculator. On the calculator part, the TI-30XS follows the order of operations exactly as written, so if you mean a negative base, you must type the parentheses.
ask: Test (x<sup>3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> with x = 2. Which is it equal to, x<sup>5</sup> or x<sup>6</sup>? (expected answer: (2<sup>3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 64 = 2<sup>6</sup>, so x<sup>6</sup>; 2<sup>5</sup> = 32 does not match)
notes.watch: Students who plug in x = 1 get every choice equal to 1 and decide the strategy does not work. Insist on 2 or 3.

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
This lesson teaches the shorthand for repeated multiplication (exponents), how to undo it (roots), and how to write very large and very small numbers in a short form (scientific notation). These skills appear all over the GED math test, and many of them show up on the first part, where you cannot use a calculator.

Work through one screen at a time. Most screens teach one rule, show a worked example, and end with a quick check you answer before moving on. Keep paper and a pencil next to you and write every step.

By the end, you will be able to:

  • Evaluate powers, including powers of negative numbers and zero and negative exponents.
  • Simplify expressions with the product, quotient, and power rules.
  • Find square roots and cube roots, estimate roots, and simplify square roots.
  • Convert, compare, multiply, and divide numbers in scientific notation.
  • Use the order of operations with exponents and roots.

Do not use a calculator until the lesson tells you to.

screens.title: Base and Exponent
screens.html:
An exponent tells you how many times to use a number, called the base, as a factor.

Key idea: 43 = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. The base is 4 and the exponent is 3. It does not mean 4 × 3.

The whole expression is called a power. Read 42 as “4 squared,” 43 as “4 cubed,” and 45 as “4 to the fifth power.” Any number to the first power is itself: 41 = 4.

To evaluate a power, write out the factors and multiply two at a time. Keep a running total so you do not lose your place.

steps: Multiply two at a time: 6 × 6 = 36, then 36 × 6 = 216.

mistakes.why: You multiplied the base by the exponent (3 × 4). The exponent counts factors: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3.
You added the base and the exponent (3 + 4). The exponent tells how many 3s to multiply together.
You switched the base and the exponent and found 4<sup>3</sup>. Here the base is 3, used as a factor 4 times.

check.hint: Write four 3s and multiply them two at a time.
check.explain:
34 means four 3s multiplied together:

3 × 3 = 9; 9 × 3 = 27; 27 × 3 = 81.

The tempting wrong answer, 12, comes from multiplying 3 × 4. An exponent is not a multiplier; it counts factors.

screens.title: Negative Bases and Parentheses
screens.html:
An exponent applies only to what it touches, the number or the parentheses right before it.

  • (−3)2: the parentheses make −3 the base. (−3)(−3) = 9.
  • −32: the exponent touches only the 3. Square the 3, then apply the negative sign: −(3 × 3) = −9.

When the base is negative, use the sign rule from Week 1 and count the negative factors:

  • An even exponent gives a positive answer: (−2)4 = 16.
  • An odd exponent gives a negative answer: (−2)3 = −8.

Watch out: Before you evaluate, circle the base. If the negative sign is not inside parentheses, it is not part of the base.

steps: −4<sup>2</sup>: the base is 4, so 4 × 4 = 16, and the negative sign makes it −16.

mistakes.why: You treated the expression as (−2)<sup>4</sup>. Without parentheses, the exponent touches only the 2: 2<sup>4</sup> = 16, and then the negative sign makes it −16.
You multiplied the base by the exponent (2 × 4 = 8). The exponent counts factors: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, so the answer is −16.

check.hint: Circle the base first. Is the negative sign inside parentheses?
check.explain:
There are no parentheses, so the base is 2, not −2.

24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

Then apply the negative sign: −24 = −16.

The tempting wrong answer, 16, is the value of (−2)4. The parentheses make all the difference.

screens.title: Powers of 10, Fractions, and Decimals
screens.html:
Powers of 10 are the easiest powers to find: the exponent tells how many zeros follow the 1.

102 = 100   103 = 1,000   106 = 1,000,000 (one million)

Fractions: a power of a fraction applies to the top and the bottom. (2/3)2 = (2 × 2)/(3 × 3) = 4/9.

Decimals: multiply as usual and count decimal places. 0.32 = 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09 (two decimal places).

Key idea: squaring a number between 0 and 1 makes it smaller. 1/2 squared is 1/4, and a quarter is less than a half.

check.prompt: Evaluate (3/4)2. Enter a fraction or a decimal.

mistakes.why: You multiplied the fraction by 2 instead of squaring it. Squaring means 3/4 × 3/4.
You squared the top but not the bottom. The exponent applies to both: 3<sup>2</sup>/4<sup>2</sup> = 9/16.
You squared the bottom but not the top. The exponent applies to both: 3<sup>2</sup>/4<sup>2</sup> = 9/16.

check.hint: Square the top and square the bottom.
check.explain:
(3/4)2 = 3/4 × 3/4 = (3 × 3)/(4 × 4) = 9/16 (0.5625).

Sense check: 9/16 is a little more than 1/2, which is smaller than 3/4, as it should be when you square a number between 0 and 1.

A common mistake is 9/4: squaring only the top.

screens.title: The Product Rule
screens.html:
When you multiply powers with the same base, keep the base and add the exponents.

Product rule: xa · xb = xa+b

Why? x2 · x3 = (x · x)(x · x · x). That is five x's, so x5. If you ever forget the rule, write the factors out and count.

Numbers in front of a variable, called coefficients, are multiplied as usual: 2x3 · 5x4 = 10x7.

Watch out: The rule needs the same base and multiplication. 23 · 32 cannot become one power (just evaluate: 8 × 9 = 72), and 23 + 22 is 8 + 4 = 12, not 25.

steps: Same base a, multiplying, so add the exponents: 3 + 5 = 8.

check.prompt: Write 23 · 22 as a single power of 2, then find its value. Enter the value.

mistakes.why: You multiplied the exponents (3 × 2 = 6) and found 2<sup>6</sup>. When you multiply powers with the same base, add the exponents: 2<sup>5</sup>.
You multiplied the bases too (2 × 2 = 4) and found 4<sup>5</sup>. Keep the base the same: 2<sup>5</sup> = 32.
You added the values 8 + 4. The dot means multiply: 8 × 4 = 32.

check.hint: Same base, multiplying: keep the base and add the exponents.
check.explain:
Same base, multiplying, so add the exponents: 23 · 22 = 23+2 = 25.

25 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.

Check: 23 = 8 and 22 = 4, and 8 × 4 = 32. The tempting wrong answer, 64, comes from multiplying the exponents.

screens.title: The Quotient Rule
screens.html:
When you divide powers with the same base, keep the base and subtract the exponents (top minus bottom).

Quotient rule: xa ÷ xb = xa−b

Why? x5 ÷ x2 = (x · x · x · x · x)/(x · x). Two x's on the bottom cancel two on the top, leaving x3.

Coefficients divide as usual: 12x7 ÷ 4x2 = 3x5.

Watch out: Subtract the exponents; do not divide them. y8 ÷ y2 = y6, not y4.

steps: Same base m, dividing, so subtract the exponents: 9 − 3 = 6.

check.prompt: Write 212 ÷ 24 as a single power of 2, then find its value. Enter the value.

mistakes.why: You divided the exponents (12 ÷ 4 = 3) and found 2<sup>3</sup>. Dividing powers with the same base subtracts the exponents: 12 − 4 = 8.
You added the exponents (12 + 4 = 16). That is the rule for multiplying. For dividing, subtract: 2<sup>8</sup>.
You divided the bases (2 ÷ 2 = 1) and got 1<sup>8</sup>. The base stays 2; only the exponents change.

check.hint: Same base, dividing: keep the base and subtract the exponents.
check.explain:
Same base, dividing, so subtract: 212 ÷ 24 = 212−4 = 28.

28: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256.

The tempting wrong answer, 8, comes from dividing the exponents instead of subtracting them.

screens.title: The Power Rule
screens.html:
When a power is raised to another power, keep the base and multiply the exponents.

Power rule: (xa)b = xab    Power of a product: (xy)a = xaya

Why? (x2)3 = x2 · x2 · x2, which is six x's, so x6.

When there is a product inside the parentheses, the outside exponent goes to every factor, including the number: (2x3)2 = 22 · x6 = 4x6.

Memory check: multiplying powers adds exponents; a power of a power multiplies them.

steps: The exponent 3 goes to both factors: 5<sup>3</sup> and (y<sup>4</sup>)<sup>3</sup>.

why: You squared the x<sup>4</sup> but not the 3. The outside exponent goes to every factor: 3<sup>2</sup> = 9.
You added the exponents (4 + 2). A power of a power multiplies them: x<sup>4×2</sup> = x<sup>8</sup>.
You multiplied 3 by 2 instead of squaring it. 3<sup>2</sup> = 3 × 3 = 9.
check.hint: The outside exponent applies to the 3 and to x<sup>4</sup>.
check.explain:
The exponent 2 goes to both factors: 32 = 9 and (x4)2 = x8.

So (3x4)2 = 9x8.

The most common wrong answer is 3x8, which forgets to square the coefficient.

screens.title: The Zero Exponent
screens.html:
Any nonzero number raised to the zero power equals 1.

Zero exponent: x0 = 1 (when x ≠ 0)

Two ways to see why:

  • Pattern: 23 = 8, 22 = 4, 21 = 2. Each step divides by 2, so the next one is 2 ÷ 2 = 1. That is 20.
  • Quotient rule: 53 ÷ 53 = 53−3 = 50. But anything divided by itself is 1.

Watch what the zero exponent touches. In 3x0, only x is raised to zero, so 3x0 = 3 · 1 = 3. In (3x)0, everything inside is raised to zero, so (3x)0 = 1.

steps: (−8)<sup>0</sup> = 1, because any nonzero number to the zero power is 1, even a negative one.

mistakes.why: You treated each zero power as 0. Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1: 7<sup>0</sup> = 1 and 4<sup>0</sup> = 1.
You raised 3 · 4 to the zero power. The exponent touches only the 4, so 3 · 4<sup>0</sup> = 3 · 1 = 3.
You treated each zero power as the number itself (7 + 3 · 4). A zero exponent gives 1, not the base.

check.hint: Each zero power equals 1. Then multiply before you add.
check.explain:
70 = 1 and 40 = 1.

The expression becomes 1 + 3 · 1 = 1 + 3 = 4.

The tempting wrong answer, 0, comes from thinking a zero exponent makes the number 0.

screens.title: Negative Exponents
screens.html:
Keep the pattern going past zero: each step down divides by 2.

21 = 2   20 = 1   2−1 = 1/2   2−2 = 1/4   2−3 = 1/8

Negative exponent: x−n = 1/xn. A negative exponent means take the reciprocal of the positive power.

A negative exponent does not make the number negative. 2−3 is 1/8, a small positive number.

Powers of 10 with negative exponents are decimals: 10−1 = 0.1, 10−2 = 0.01, 10−3 = 0.001. You will use these in scientific notation.

The other rules still work: x3 · x−5 = x3+(−5) = x−2 = 1/x2.

steps: Take the reciprocal of the positive power: 3<sup>−2</sup> = 1/3<sup>2</sup>.

check.prompt: Evaluate 4−3. Enter a fraction or a decimal.

mistakes.why: You made the answer negative. A negative exponent means reciprocal: 4<sup>−3</sup> = 1/4<sup>3</sup> = 1/64, which is positive.
You multiplied 4 × (−3). An exponent counts factors, and a negative exponent means reciprocal: 1/(4 × 4 × 4).
You took the reciprocal correctly but multiplied 4 × 3 instead of finding 4<sup>3</sup> = 64.

check.hint: Write the reciprocal of the positive power, then evaluate the power.
check.explain:
4−3 = 1/43.

43 = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

So 4−3 = 1/64 (0.015625).

The tempting wrong answer, −64, treats the negative exponent as a negative sign on the answer.

screens.title: Square Roots and Perfect Squares
screens.html:
A square root undoes squaring. √49 = 7 because 72 = 49. On the GED, the symbol √ means the positive root.

A perfect square is a whole number whose square root is a whole number. Learn these by heart; the no-calculator part of the test depends on them.

n123456789101112131415
n2149162536496481100121144169196225

The square root of a negative number, such as √(−16), is not a real number, because no real number times itself is negative.

Watch out: A square root is not half. √64 = 8, not 32.

steps: Ask: what number times itself is 196?

mistakes.why: You added under one root: √(144 + 25) = √169 = 13. These are two separate roots: 12 + 5 = 17.
You divided each number by 2 (72 + 12.5). A square root asks what number times itself gives the number: 12 × 12 = 144.

check.hint: Find each square root separately, then add.
check.explain:
√144 = 12 because 12 × 12 = 144.

√25 = 5 because 5 × 5 = 25.

12 + 5 = 17.

Halving the numbers (72 + 12.5) is the most common root mistake.

screens.title: Estimating Square Roots
screens.html:
Most numbers are not perfect squares, so their square roots are not whole numbers. You can still estimate them without a calculator.

  1. Find the perfect squares just below and just above the number.
  2. The root is between their square roots.
  3. Decide which end it is closer to.

For example, √30: since 25 < 30 < 36, √30 is between 5 and 6. 30 is 5 away from 25 and 6 away from 36, so √30 is a little closer to 5. A calculator gives 5.477….

The GED often asks, “Between which two consecutive whole numbers is √55?” Consecutive means one right after the other, like 7 and 8.

example.prompt: Between which two consecutive whole numbers is √55?

check.prompt:
Choose the numbers that make the statement true.

√130 is between {{0}} and {{1}}, and it is closer to {{2}}.

why: 10<sup>2</sup> = 100, but 11<sup>2</sup> = 121 is also less than 130. Use the closest perfect square below 130, which is 121.
12<sup>2</sup> = 144 is more than 130, so 12 is the upper number, not the lower one.
You divided 130 by 2. A square root is not half: 65 × 65 = 4,225.
11 is the lower number. You need the next whole number whose square is more than 130.
13<sup>2</sup> = 169, but 12<sup>2</sup> = 144 is already more than 130. Use the closest perfect square above 130.
You worked with half of 130. A square root is not half: compare 130 with the perfect squares 121 and 144.
130 is 9 away from 121 but 14 away from 144, so the root is closer to 11 (it is about 11.4).
130 is not halfway between 121 and 144 (the halfway point is 132.5), so the root is not halfway between 11 and 12.

check.hint: Which perfect squares are just below and just above 130?
check.explain:
112 = 121 and 122 = 144, and 121 < 130 < 144.

So √130 is between 11 and 12.

130 − 121 = 9 and 144 − 130 = 14, so 130 is closer to 121, and √130 is closer to 11. A calculator gives about 11.40.

screens.title: Simplifying Square Roots
screens.html:
When a square root is not a whole number, the GED may ask for it in simplest form. You can split a root across multiplication: √(a × b) = √a × √b.

  1. Find the largest perfect square that divides the number.
  2. Write the number as that perfect square times what is left.
  3. Take the square root of the perfect square and write it in front.

√50 = √(25 × 2) = √25 × √2 = 5√2.

Check by squaring: (5√2)2 = 25 × 2 = 50.

Watch out: You can split a root across multiplication, but never across addition. √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10, not 6 + 8 = 14.

steps: Perfect squares that divide 72: 4, 9, and 36. The largest is 36.

why: You used the perfect square 4: √80 = 2√20. That is equal to √80 but not finished, because 20 still has the perfect-square factor 4. Use the largest one, 16.
You pulled 16 out of the root without taking its square root. √16 = 4, so the answer is 4√5. Check: (16√5)<sup>2</sup> = 1,280, not 80.
You pulled out 8, but 8 is not a perfect square, and you did not take its root. (8√10)<sup>2</sup> = 640, not 80.
check.hint: What is the largest perfect square that divides 80?
check.explain:
Perfect squares that divide 80: 4 and 16. The largest is 16.

√80 = √(16 × 5) = √16 × √5 = 4√5.

Check: (4√5)2 = 16 × 5 = 80.

2√20 has the right value, but it is not in simplest form because √20 can still be simplified.

screens.title: Cube Roots
screens.html:
A cube root undoes cubing. ∛125 = 5 because 53 = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.

n1234510
n31827641251,000

Unlike square roots, cube roots of negative numbers are real: ∛(−8) = −2, because (−2)(−2)(−2) = −8. A negative number has a negative cube root.

Watch out: Do not mix up the two roots. √64 = 8, but ∛64 = 4. And a cube root is not dividing by 3: ∛27 = 3, not 9.

mistakes.why: You took ∛(−64) as 4. The cube root of a negative number is negative: (−4)<sup>3</sup> = −64, so ∛(−64) = −4.
You used 8, the square root of 64, for ∛(−64). The cube root of 64 is 4, because 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

check.hint: Which number, used as a factor three times, gives −64? Which gives 27?
check.explain:
∛(−64) = −4, because (−4)(−4)(−4) = 16 × (−4) = −64.

∛27 = 3, because 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.

−4 + 3 = −1.

The tempting wrong answer, 7, drops the negative sign of the first cube root.

screens.title: Writing Numbers in Scientific Notation
screens.html:
Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10n, where a is at least 1 and less than 10, and n is an integer. It is used for very large numbers (distances in space, populations, budgets) and very small numbers (cells, bacteria).

Steps:

  1. Move the decimal point so exactly one nonzero digit is to its left.
  2. Count how many places you moved it. That is the size of the exponent.
  3. If the original number is 10 or more, the exponent is positive. If it is less than 1, the exponent is negative.

Examples: 93,000,000 = 9.3 × 107 (7 places). 0.000002 = 2 × 10−6 (6 places).

Count the moves, not the zeros. In 0.000002 there are five zeros after the point, but the point moves six places to get to 2.

steps: 4,500,000 → 4.5: the point moves 6 places left. The number is large, so the exponent is positive: 4.5 × 10<sup>6</sup>.
0.00031 → 3.1: the point moves 4 places right. The number is less than 1, so the exponent is negative: 3.1 × 10<sup>−4</sup>.

mistakes.why: You counted the moves correctly but gave the wrong sign. 0.00056 is less than 1, so the exponent is negative.
You counted the zeros after the decimal point (three). Count the moves instead: the point moves 4 places to get from 0.00056 to 5.6.

check.hint: Count how many places the decimal point moves to get to 5.6. Is the number bigger or smaller than 1?
check.explain:
Move the decimal point to the right until one nonzero digit is in front: 0.00056 → 5.6. That is 4 moves.

The number is less than 1, so the exponent is negative: 0.00056 = 5.6 × 10−4, and n = −4.

Check: 5.6 × 10−4 = 5.6 × 0.0001 = 0.00056.

screens.title: From Scientific Notation to Standard Form
screens.html:
Standard form is the usual way of writing a number with all its digits. To change scientific notation to standard form, move the decimal point the number of places the exponent tells you.

  • Positive exponent: move the point to the right (the number gets bigger). Fill empty places with zeros.
  • Negative exponent: move the point to the left (the number gets smaller). Fill empty places with zeros.

A quick check: 103 = 1,000, so 6.4 × 103 = 6.4 × 1,000 = 6,400. And 10−3 = 0.001, so 6.4 × 10−3 = 0.0064.

Watch out: The exponent is the number of places the point moves, not the number of zeros you add. 3.25 × 104 = 32,500, which has only two zeros.

check.prompt: A large city has about 3.07 × 105 households. Write this number in standard form.

mistakes.why: You wrote five zeros after 307. Move the decimal point 5 places instead: 3.07 → 307,000. The digits 0 and 7 use up two of the five places.
You moved the decimal point to the left. A positive exponent means a large number, so move the point to the right.
You moved the decimal point only 4 places. The exponent is 5, so move it 5 places: 307,000.

check.hint: A positive exponent of 5 means move the decimal point 5 places to the right.
check.explain:
105 = 100,000, so 3.07 × 105 = 3.07 × 100,000.

Move the decimal point 5 places to the right: 3.07 → 30.7 → 307. → 3,070. → 30,700. → 307,000.

A common mistake is to tack five zeros onto 307, giving 30,700,000.

screens.title: Comparing Numbers in Scientific Notation
screens.html:
To compare two numbers in scientific notation, look at the exponents first. Each step up in the exponent multiplies by 10, which outweighs any difference in the front numbers.

  • Different exponents: the greater exponent wins. 2 × 105 (200,000) > 9 × 104 (90,000).
  • Same exponent: compare the front numbers. 7.1 × 103 > 6.8 × 103.
  • Negative exponents: −6 is less than −4, so 5 × 10−6 < 1 × 10−4.

If you are unsure, write both numbers in standard form and compare place by place.

example.prompt: Which is smaller: 8 × 10<sup>−6</sup> m (a red blood cell) or 3 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m (a skin cell)?
steps: So 8 × 10<sup>−6</sup> is smaller, even though 8 > 3. In standard form: 0.000008 < 0.00003.
example.answer: The red blood cell, 8 × 10<sup>−6</sup> m, is smaller.

why: You compared the front numbers first. 9.8 × 10<sup>4</sup> = 98,000, but 1.2 × 10<sup>5</sup> = 120,000 has the greater exponent.
9.9 has the largest front number, but the exponent 3 makes it only 9,900. Compare the exponents first.
You may have looked at the 6 and ignored its negative sign. 10<sup>−6</sup> makes this a tiny number: 0.000005.
check.hint: Compare the exponents first. Only compare front numbers when the exponents match.
check.explain:
The exponents are 4, 5, 3, and −6. The greatest exponent is 5, so 1.2 × 105 is the greatest.

In standard form: 120,000 > 98,000 > 9,900 > 0.000005.

The tempting wrong choice is 9.8 × 104, because 9.8 looks bigger than 1.2.

screens.title: Multiplying in Scientific Notation
screens.html:
To multiply numbers in scientific notation, work with the two parts separately.

  1. Multiply the front numbers.
  2. Add the exponents (the product rule with base 10).
  3. Adjust if the front number is 10 or more: divide it by 10 and add 1 to the exponent.

Balance idea: 15 × 1010 = 1.5 × 1011. The front number got 10 times smaller, so the power of 10 must get 10 times bigger.

Word problems use multiplication when you combine a rate with an amount: cells per microliter times microliters, or bytes per photo times photos.

steps: 15 is not less than 10. Rewrite 15 as 1.5 × 10<sup>1</sup>: 1.5 × 10<sup>1</sup> × 10<sup>10</sup> = 1.5 × 10<sup>11</sup>.

mistakes.why: You added the exponents to get 24 × 10<sup>8</sup> but did not adjust. 24 = 2.4 × 10<sup>1</sup>, so the exponent goes up by 1: 10<sup>9</sup>.
You multiplied the exponents (5 × 3). When you multiply powers of 10, add the exponents: 5 + 3 = 8, then adjust.
You adjusted in the wrong direction. Making the front number 10 times smaller (24 to 2.4) makes the exponent 1 bigger: 8 + 1 = 9.

check.hint: Multiply the fronts, add the exponents, then make the front number between 1 and 10.
check.explain:
Front numbers: 4 × 6 = 24. Exponents: 5 + 3 = 8. So far: 24 × 108.

Adjust: 24 = 2.4 × 101, so 24 × 108 = 2.4 × 109, and n = 9.

Check: 400,000 × 6,000 = 2,400,000,000 = 2.4 × 109.

screens.title: Dividing in Scientific Notation
screens.html:
To divide numbers in scientific notation, again work with the parts separately.

  1. Divide the front numbers.
  2. Subtract the exponents (top minus bottom).
  3. Adjust if the front number is less than 1: multiply it by 10 and subtract 1 from the exponent.

Word problems use division for “how many times greater,” “how many fit,” “per person,” and time = distance ÷ speed.

Strategy: Before dividing, decide which number goes on top. The answer to “how many times greater is A than B?” is A ÷ B, and it should be more than 1.

example.prompt: The world population is about 8 × 10<sup>9</sup>. A large city has about 4 × 10<sup>6</sup> people. How many times greater is the world population?
steps: Divide the front numbers: 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Subtract the exponents: 9 − 6 = 3.

check.prompt: Find (1.2 × 106) ÷ (4 × 102). Enter the answer in standard form.

mistakes.why: You changed 0.3 to 3 without adjusting the exponent (3 × 10<sup>4</sup>). Making the front number 10 times bigger means making the exponent 1 smaller: 3 × 10<sup>3</sup>.
You adjusted in the wrong direction (3 × 10<sup>5</sup>). 0.3 × 10<sup>4</sup> = 3 × 10<sup>3</sup>, because the front got bigger, so the exponent gets smaller.
You multiplied (4.8 × 10<sup>8</sup>). This problem divides: divide the fronts and subtract the exponents.

check.hint: Divide the fronts, subtract the exponents, then make the front number between 1 and 10.
check.explain:
Front numbers: 1.2 ÷ 4 = 0.3. Exponents: 6 − 2 = 4. So far: 0.3 × 104.

Adjust: 0.3 = 3 × 10−1, so 0.3 × 104 = 3 × 103 = 3,000.

Check: 1,200,000 ÷ 400 = 3,000. The tempting wrong answer, 30,000, skips the adjustment of the exponent.

screens.title: Order of Operations with Exponents and Roots
screens.html:
Here is the full order of operations you started in Week 1, with exponents and roots in their place:

  1. Grouping symbols: ( ), [ ], | |, fraction bars, and everything under a root symbol
  2. Exponents and roots
  3. Multiplication and division, left to right
  4. Addition and subtraction, left to right

An exponent belongs only to what it touches. In 2 × 32, square the 3 first: 2 × 9 = 18, not 62 = 36.

The root bar groups: in √(16 + 9), add first: √25 = 5. Rewrite the whole expression after every step so nothing gets lost.

steps: Divide and multiply left to right: 36 ÷ 4 = 9, then 9 × 3 = 27. Now: 2 + 27.

check.skill: Order of operations with exponents and roots

mistakes.why: You split the root across the addition: √16 + √9 = 4 + 3 = 7. The root bar groups: add first, √25 = 5.
You added 3 + 5 before subtracting (30 − 8). Add and subtract from left to right: 30 − 3 = 27, then 27 + 5 = 32.

check.hint: Work inside the parentheses and under the root first. Then exponents and roots, then divide, then add and subtract left to right.
check.explain:
Grouping: 2 + 1 = 3 and 16 + 9 = 25. Now: 30 − 33 ÷ 9 + √25.

Exponents and roots: 33 = 27 and √25 = 5. Now: 30 − 27 ÷ 9 + 5.

Divide: 27 ÷ 9 = 3. Now: 30 − 3 + 5.

Left to right: 30 − 3 = 27; 27 + 5 = 32.

The tempting wrong answer, 34, comes from splitting the root: √(16 + 9) is not √16 + √9.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• An exponent counts factors: 43 = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, not 12.
  • The exponent touches only what is next to it: (−3)2 = 9, but −32 = −9.
  • Same base: multiplying adds exponents, dividing subtracts them, and a power of a power multiplies them. An outside exponent goes to every factor: (2x3)2 = 4x6.
  • x0 = 1 (x ≠ 0). x−n = 1/xn: a reciprocal, not a negative number.
  • Square roots undo squaring and cube roots undo cubing. ∛(−8) = −2; √(−16) is not a real number.
  • Estimate a root between perfect squares. Simplify by pulling out the largest perfect square: √50 = 5√2. Never split a root across addition.
  • Scientific notation: a × 10n with 1 ≤ a < 10. Large numbers get positive exponents; numbers less than 1 get negative exponents.
  • Multiply: multiply fronts, add exponents. Divide: divide fronts, subtract exponents. Then adjust. Compare exponents first.
  • Order: grouping (including under a root), exponents and roots, multiply and divide left to right, add and subtract left to right.

Next: Practice Set A. If you score under 80%, practice the same skills again with Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

items.prompt: What is the value of 25?
why: You multiplied the base by the exponent (2 × 5). The exponent counts factors: five 2s multiplied together.
You switched the base and the exponent and found 5<sup>2</sup>. Here the base is 2, used as a factor 5 times.
You added the base and the exponent (2 + 5). An exponent means repeated multiplication, not addition.
items.hint: The exponent tells how many 2s to multiply together.
items.explain:
25 means five 2s multiplied together:

2 × 2 = 4

4 × 2 = 8

8 × 2 = 16

16 × 2 = 32

The choice 10 comes from multiplying the base by the exponent (2 × 5). The choice 25 comes from switching the base and exponent (52). The choice 7 comes from adding 2 + 5.

items.prompt: Evaluate √49 + ∛64.

mistakes.why: You used 8, the square root of 64, for the cube root. ∛64 asks what number used as a factor three times gives 64: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.
You added 49 + 64 and ignored the root symbols. Take each root first: 7 + 4.

items.hint: Which number times itself is 49? Which number used three times as a factor is 64?
items.explain:
√49 = 7, because 7 × 7 = 49.

∛64 = 4, because 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

7 + 4 = 11.

The most tempting wrong answer, 15, mixes up the two roots: 8 is the square root of 64, not the cube root.

items.prompt:
The population of a small city is about 5.2 × 104 people.

Write this number in standard form.

mistakes.why: You wrote four zeros after 52. The exponent tells how many places to move the decimal point, and the 2 already uses one of the four places: 5.2 → 52,000.

You moved the decimal point to the left. A positive exponent means a large number, so move it to the right.

104 = 10,000, so 5.2 × 104 = 5.2 × 10,000.

Move the decimal point in 5.2 four places to the right, filling empty places with zeros:

5.2 → 52. → 520. → 5,200. → 52,000.

The population is 52,000 people.

A common mistake is to write 520,000 by adding four zeros after 52 instead of moving the decimal point four places.

items.prompt:
A grain of pollen is about 0.000025 meter wide. In scientific notation, this width is 2.5 × 10n meter.

What is the value of n?

mistakes.why: You counted the moves correctly but gave the exponent the wrong sign. The width is less than 1 meter, so the exponent is negative.
You counted the four zeros after the decimal point. Count the moves instead: the point moves 5 places to get from 0.000025 to 2.5.
You counted all six digits after the decimal point. The point stops after the 2, so it moves only 5 places.

items.hint: Count how many places the decimal point moves to get to 2.5. Is the number bigger or smaller than 1?
items.explain:
Move the decimal point right until one nonzero digit is in front of it: 0.000025 → 2.5. That is 5 moves.

The number is less than 1, so the exponent is negative: 0.000025 = 2.5 × 10−5, so n = −5.

Check: 2.5 × 10−5 = 2.5 × 0.00001 = 0.000025.

The tempting wrong answer, −4, counts the zeros instead of the moves.

items.skill: Negative bases and order of operations
items.prompt: Evaluate −24 + 3(−2)2.

mistakes.why: You treated −2<sup>4</sup> as (−2)<sup>4</sup> = 16. Without parentheses the exponent touches only the 2, so −2<sup>4</sup> = −16.
You treated (−2)<sup>2</sup> as −4. With parentheses the base is −2: (−2)(−2) = 4, so 3(−2)<sup>2</sup> = 12.
You multiplied 3 × (−2) before squaring: (−6)<sup>2</sup> = 36. Exponents come before multiplication: (−2)<sup>2</sup> = 4, then 3 × 4 = 12.

items.hint: Find the base of each power first. Then do exponents, then multiplication, then addition.
items.explain:
First power: no parentheses, so the base is 2. 24 = 16, so −24 = −16.

Second power: the base is −2. (−2)2 = 4, and 3 × 4 = 12.

Add: −16 + 12 = −4.

The most common wrong answer, 28, treats both powers as having a negative base.

items.prompt: Which expression is equivalent to 3x4 · 2x3?
why: You added the coefficients (3 + 2 = 5). The dot means multiply, so multiply the coefficients: 3 × 2 = 6.
You multiplied the exponents (4 × 3 = 12). When you multiply powers with the same base, add the exponents: 4 + 3 = 7.
You mixed up both rules: you added the coefficients and multiplied the exponents. Multiply the coefficients (6) and add the exponents (7).
items.hint: Multiply the numbers in front. For the same base, add the exponents.
items.explain:
Multiply the coefficients: 3 × 2 = 6.

Multiply the powers of x. The bases are the same, so add the exponents: x4 · x3 = x4+3 = x7.

The product is 6x7.

Check with x = 2 (not x = 1, because every power of 1 is 1): 3(16) · 2(8) = 48 × 16 = 768, and 6(27) = 6 × 128 = 768.

The choice 6x12 comes from multiplying the exponents instead of adding them. The choices with 5 come from adding the coefficients instead of multiplying.

items.prompt: Evaluate 5−2. Enter a fraction or a decimal.

mistakes.why: You made the answer negative. A negative exponent means reciprocal: 5<sup>−2</sup> = 1/5<sup>2</sup> = 1/25, a positive number.
You multiplied 5 × (−2). The exponent counts factors, and the negative sign means reciprocal: 1/(5 × 5).
You took the reciprocal but multiplied 5 × 2 instead of squaring. 5<sup>2</sup> = 25, so the answer is 1/25.

items.hint: A negative exponent means take the reciprocal of the positive power.
items.explain:
5−2 = 1/52 = 1/(5 × 5) = 1/25, which is 0.04.

The tempting wrong answer, −25, treats the negative exponent as a negative sign. A negative exponent makes a reciprocal, and the value stays positive.

items.prompt: The approximate sizes (length or diameter) of four cells are listed below, in meters. Drag each cell into its position so the cells are in order from smallest (1st) to largest (4th).
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the red blood cell (8 × 10<sup>−6</sup>) last because 8 is the largest front number, or putting the egg cell (1.2 × 10<sup>−4</sup>) first because 1.2 is the smallest. Compare the exponents first: −6 < −5 < −4.

items.explain:
Compare the exponents first. A more negative exponent means a smaller number: 10−6 < 10−5 < 10−4.

Two cells have the exponent −6. Compare the front numbers: 2 < 8, so the E. coli bacterium (2 × 10−6) is smaller than the red blood cell (8 × 10−6).

In standard form: 0.000002 < 0.000008 < 0.00003 < 0.00012.

Order: E. coli bacterium, red blood cell, skin cell, human egg cell.

A common mistake is to put the red blood cell last because 8 is the biggest front number. The exponent matters more than the front number.

items.prompt: Which expression is √108 in simplest form?
why: You pulled 36 out of the root without taking its square root. √36 = 6. Check: (36√3)<sup>2</sup> = 3,888, not 108.
You used the perfect square 9: √108 = 3√12. That has the right value but is not finished, because 12 still has the perfect-square factor 4. Use the largest perfect square, 36.
You put the wrong factor outside. In 108 = 12 × 9, the perfect square is 9, so its root comes out, not the 12. And 12√9 = 12 × 3 = 36, not √108.
items.hint: Find the largest perfect square that divides 108.
items.explain:
Perfect squares that divide 108: 4, 9, and 36. The largest is 36.

108 = 36 × 3, so √108 = √36 × √3 = 6√3.

Check: (6√3)2 = 36 × 3 = 108.

3√12 is equal to √108 but is not in simplest form, because √12 = 2√3 can still be simplified.

items.prompt: Select two expressions that are equal to 1/16.
why: (−4)<sup>2</sup> = (−4)(−4) = 16. A negative base is not a negative exponent: there is no reciprocal here.
−4<sup>2</sup> = −(4 × 4) = −16. The negative sign makes the answer negative; it does not make a reciprocal.
16<sup>0</sup> = 1. Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1, not 1/16.
8<sup>−2</sup> = 1/8<sup>2</sup> = 1/64. You may have multiplied 8 × 2 = 16 instead of squaring 8.
items.hint: Evaluate each one. A negative exponent gives a reciprocal; a zero exponent gives 1.
items.explain:
Evaluate each expression:

  • 4−2 = 1/42 = 1/16 Correct
  • 2−4 = 1/24 = 1/16 Correct
  • (−4)2 = (−4)(−4) = 16
  • −42 = −(4 × 4) = −16
  • 160 = 1
  • 8−2 = 1/82 = 1/64

The two expressions equal to 1/16 are 4−2 and 2−4.

−42 and (−4)2 are tempting because they use the digits 4 and 2, but neither has a negative exponent, so neither produces a reciprocal: they equal −16 and 16, not 1/16. Remember that a negative exponent means a reciprocal, and a negative sign on the base is a different thing.

items.prompt:
A human hair is about 6 × 10−5 meter wide. A flu virus is about 1.2 × 10−7 meter wide.

About how many times wider is the hair than the virus?

You divided the virus by the hair. “How many times wider is the hair” means hair ÷ virus, and the answer must be more than 1.
You multiplied the widths (6 × 1.2 = 7.2 and −5 + −7 = −12). Comparing how many times wider means divide.

Times wider = hair ÷ virus = (6 × 10−5) ÷ (1.2 × 10−7).

Front numbers: 6 ÷ 1.2 = 5.

Exponents: −5 − (−7) = −5 + 7 = 2.

The result is 5 × 102, so the hair is about 500 times wider.

items.skill: Order of operations with exponents and roots
items.prompt:

52 − 2(3 − 7)2 ÷ 8 + ∛(−64)

Parentheses first: 3 − 7 = −4. The expression is 52 − 2(−4)2 ÷ 8 + ∛(−64)

52 = 25

(−4)2 = (−4)(−4) = 16

∛(−64) = −4, because (−4)(−4)(−4) = −64

A data center has about 2.5 × 104 servers. Each server stores about 8 × 1012 bytes of data.

You multiplied the exponents (4 × 12). When you multiply powers of 10, add the exponents: 4 + 12 = 16, then adjust.

Front numbers: 2.5 × 8 = 20. Exponents: 4 + 12 = 16. So far: 20 × 1016.

Adjust: 20 = 2 × 101, so the total is 2 × 1017 bytes, and n = 17.

items.prompt:

To the nearest tenth of a foot, how many feet of edging are needed? You may use a calculator.

∛27 = 3 because 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.

9 + 3 = 12

Write this mass in standard form.

You moved the decimal point only 3 places. The exponent is −4, so move it 4 places to the left: 0.00046.

items.prompt:
The population of the world is about 8,100,000,000 people. In scientific notation, this is 8.1 × 10n.

What is the value of n?

mistakes.why: You counted the eight zeros. Count the moves instead: the decimal point moves 9 places to get from 8,100,000,000 to 8.1.
You counted correctly but used a negative exponent. The number is much larger than 10, so the exponent is positive.
You counted all ten digits. The decimal point stops after the 8, so it moves 9 places.

items.hint: Count how many places the decimal point moves left to get to 8.1.
items.explain:
The decimal point is at the end: 8,100,000,000. Move it left until one nonzero digit is in front: 8.100000000. That is 9 moves.

The number is large, so the exponent is positive: 8.1 × 109, and n = 9.

Check: 109 is one billion, and 8.1 billion is 8,100,000,000. The tempting wrong answer, 8, counts zeros instead of moves.

items.prompt: Evaluate 3 + 2 × 42 using the order of operations.
why: You added first: (3 + 2) × 16 = 80. Addition comes last. Multiply 2 × 16 first, then add 3.
You multiplied before squaring: (2 × 4)<sup>2</sup> = 64, then 3 + 64 = 67. The exponent touches only the 4: 4<sup>2</sup> = 16.
You treated 4<sup>2</sup> as 4 × 2 = 8, so 3 + 16 = 19. 4<sup>2</sup> = 4 × 4 = 16.
items.hint: Exponents come before multiplication, and multiplication comes before addition.
items.explain:
Exponent first: 42 = 16. The expression is 3 + 2 × 16.

Multiply next: 2 × 16 = 32. The expression is 3 + 32.

Add: 3 + 32 = 35

The choice 80 comes from adding first: (3 + 2) × 16. The choice 67 comes from multiplying before squaring: 3 + (2 × 4)2 = 3 + 64. The choice 19 comes from treating 42 as 4 × 2 = 8.

items.prompt: Write 42 · 43 as a single power of 4, then find its value. Enter the value.

mistakes.why: You multiplied the exponents (2 × 3 = 6) and found 4<sup>6</sup>. When you multiply powers with the same base, add the exponents: 4<sup>5</sup>.
You multiplied the bases too (4 × 4 = 16) and found 16<sup>5</sup>. Keep the base the same: 4<sup>5</sup> = 1,024.
You added the values 16 + 64. The dot means multiply: 16 × 64 = 1,024.

items.hint: Same base, multiplying: keep the base and add the exponents.
items.explain:
Same base, multiplying, so add the exponents: 42 · 43 = 42+3 = 45.

45: 4, 16, 64, 256, 1,024.

Check: 42 = 16 and 43 = 64, and 16 × 64 = 1,024. The tempting wrong answer, 4,096, comes from multiplying the exponents.

items.prompt:
Choose the expression or number that makes each statement true. Assume x ≠ 0.

x9 ÷ x3 = {{0}}

(x2)5 = {{1}}

70 = {{2}}

why: You divided the exponents (9 ÷ 3). Dividing powers with the same base subtracts the exponents: 9 − 3 = 6.
You added the exponents (9 + 3). That is the rule for multiplying. For dividing, subtract.
You multiplied the exponents (9 × 3). For dividing powers with the same base, subtract: 9 − 3 = 6.
You added the exponents (2 + 5). A power raised to a power multiplies them: 2 × 5 = 10.
You squared the 5 (5<sup>2</sup> = 25). Multiply the two exponents instead: 2 × 5 = 10.
You raised 2 to the fifth power (2<sup>5</sup> = 32). Multiply the two exponents instead: 2 × 5 = 10.
A zero exponent does not make the value 0. Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1: 7<sup>0</sup> = 7<sup>2</sup> ÷ 7<sup>2</sup> = 1.
You treated 7<sup>0</sup> as 7<sup>1</sup>. Only the first power of a number is the number itself; the zero power is 1.
There is no negative sign in 7<sup>0</sup>, so the value cannot be negative. Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1.

items.hint: Dividing powers with the same base: subtract exponents. A power of a power: multiply exponents. Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1.
items.explain:
First statement: same base, dividing, so subtract the exponents: x9−3 = x6. (x3 comes from dividing 9 by 3 instead of subtracting.)

Second statement: a power of a power, so multiply the exponents: x2×5 = x10. (x7 comes from adding instead of multiplying.)

Third statement: any nonzero number to the zero power is 1, so 70 = 1. You can see why with the quotient rule: 70 = 72 ÷ 72 = 49 ÷ 49 = 1. Choosing 0 is the most common mistake.

items.prompt: What is the value of 2−3?
why: You treated the negative exponent as a negative sign on the answer. A negative exponent means reciprocal: 1/2<sup>3</sup> = 1/8.
You multiplied 2 × (−3). An exponent counts factors, and a negative exponent means reciprocal: 1/(2 × 2 × 2).
You took the reciprocal correctly but multiplied 2 × 3 instead of finding 2<sup>3</sup> = 8.
items.hint: A negative exponent means take the reciprocal of the positive power.
items.explain:
A negative exponent means the reciprocal of the positive power:

2−3 = 1/23

23 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8

So 2−3 = 1/8

The choice −8 comes from treating the negative exponent as a negative sign on the answer. The choice −6 comes from multiplying 2 × (−3). The choice 1/6 takes the reciprocal correctly but multiplies 2 × 3 instead of finding 23.

items.prompt: Four online videos had the view counts shown below. Drag each video into its position so the videos are in order from fewest views (1st) to most views (4th).
items.why: The most common mistake is ordering by the front numbers alone and putting Video P (9.1) last or Video Q (1.5) first. Compare the exponents first: 10<sup>5</sup> < 10<sup>6</sup> < 10<sup>7</sup>. Only Q and S share an exponent, so compare their front numbers: 1.5 < 2.03.
items.hint: Compare the exponents first. When two exponents match, compare the front numbers.
items.explain:
Compare the exponents first: Video R has 105, Video P has 106, and Videos Q and S have 107.

Q and S share the exponent 7, so compare the front numbers: 1.5 < 2.03, so Q has fewer views than S.

In standard form: 880,000 < 9,100,000 < 15,000,000 < 20,300,000.

Order: Video R, Video P, Video Q, Video S.

A common mistake is to put Video P last because 9.1 is the largest front number. The exponent matters more than the front number.

items.prompt: Which expression is √72 in simplest form?
why: You pulled 36 out of the root without taking its square root. √36 = 6. Check: (36√2)<sup>2</sup> = 2,592, not 72.
You split 72 as 9 × 8 and pulled out 9 without taking its root. √9 = 3, and √8 can still be simplified. Check: (9√8)<sup>2</sup> = 648, not 72.
You used the perfect square 4: √72 = 2√18. That has the right value but is not finished, because 18 still has the perfect-square factor 9. Use the largest perfect square, 36.
items.hint: Find the largest perfect square that divides 72.
items.explain:
Look for the largest perfect square that is a factor of 72. The perfect squares 4, 9, and 36 all divide 72; the largest is 36.

72 = 36 × 2

√72 = √36 × √2 = 6√2

Check: (6√2)2 = 36 × 2 = 72.

The choice 36√2 moves 36 outside without taking its square root; (36√2)2 = 2,592. The choice 9√8 makes the same mistake with 9; (9√8)2 = 648. The choice 2√18 has the right value but is not in simplest form, because √18 = 3√2 can still be simplified.

items.prompt: Select two expressions that are equal to 1/9.
why: −3<sup>2</sup> = −(3 × 3) = −9. A negative sign in front makes a negative number, not a reciprocal.
9<sup>0</sup> = 1. Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1, not 1/9.
3<sup>−3</sup> = 1/3<sup>3</sup> = 1/27. You need 3 used as a factor twice, not three times.
(1/3)<sup>−2</sup> flips 1/3 to 3, then squares it: 3<sup>2</sup> = 9. The reciprocal of a fraction is a whole number here, not 1/9.
items.hint: Evaluate each one. A negative exponent means reciprocal. A zero exponent gives 1.
items.explain:
Evaluate each expression:

  • 3−2 = 1/32 = 1/9 Correct
  • 9−1 = 1/91 = 1/9 Correct
  • −32 = −9
  • 90 = 1
  • 3−3 = 1/27
  • (1/3)−2 = 32 = 9

The two expressions equal to 1/9 are 3−2 and 9−1.

(1/3)−2 is the tricky one: a negative exponent on a fraction flips the fraction, giving 9, not 1/9.

items.prompt:
The distance from the Sun to Earth is about 1.5 × 108 kilometers. Light travels about 3.0 × 105 kilometers per second.

About how many seconds does it take light from the Sun to reach Earth?
why: You changed 0.5 to 5.0 without adjusting the exponent. Making the front number 10 times bigger means making the exponent 1 smaller: 5.0 × 10<sup>2</sup>.
You divided speed by distance. Time = distance ÷ speed, so the distance (1.5 × 10<sup>8</sup>) goes on top.
You multiplied distance by speed. Time = distance ÷ speed, so divide the front numbers and subtract the exponents.
items.hint: Time = distance ÷ speed. Divide the front numbers and subtract the exponents. Then make sure the front number is between 1 and 10.
items.explain:
Time = distance ÷ speed = (1.5 × 108) ÷ (3.0 × 105)

Divide the front numbers: 1.5 ÷ 3.0 = 0.5

Subtract the exponents: 108 ÷ 105 = 108−5 = 103

So far: 0.5 × 103. The front number 0.5 is less than 1, so rewrite 0.5 as 5 × 10−1:

5 × 10−1 × 103 = 5.0 × 102 seconds (500 seconds, a little over 8 minutes).

The choice 5.0 × 103 changes 0.5 to 5.0 without adjusting the exponent. The choice 2.0 × 10−3 divides speed by distance. The choice 4.5 × 1013 multiplies instead of dividing.

items.skill: Order of operations with exponents and roots
items.prompt:
Simplify the expression completely. Enter your answer as a single integer.

2(5 − 8)2 − √64 ÷ 4 + (−2)3

mistakes.why: You multiplied 2 × (−3) = −6 before squaring and got 36. Exponents come before multiplication: (−3)<sup>2</sup> = 9, then 2 × 9 = 18.
You took (−2)<sup>3</sup> as 8. Three negative factors, an odd number, give a negative answer: (−2)<sup>3</sup> = −8.
You divided before taking the root: √(64 ÷ 4) = √16 = 4. The root covers only the 64: √64 = 8, then 8 ÷ 4 = 2.

items.hint: Parentheses first, then every exponent and root, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract left to right.
items.explain:
Parentheses: 5 − 8 = −3. Now: 2(−3)2 − √64 ÷ 4 + (−2)3.

Exponents and roots: (−3)2 = 9, √64 = 8, and (−2)3 = −8. Now: 2 × 9 − 8 ÷ 4 + (−8).

Multiply and divide: 2 × 9 = 18 and 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Now: 18 − 2 + (−8).

Left to right: 18 − 2 = 16; 16 + (−8) = 8.

The most common mistake is 26, from multiplying 2 × (−3) before squaring.

items.prompt:
A large city's water system delivers about 4.5 × 108 gallons of water per day.

In a year of 365 days, it delivers about 1.6 × 10n gallons. What is the value of n?

mistakes.why: You found 16.4 × 10<sup>10</sup> but did not adjust. 16.4 = 1.64 × 10<sup>1</sup>, so the exponent goes up by 1: 10<sup>11</sup>.
You multiplied the exponents (8 × 2). When you multiply powers of 10, add the exponents: 8 + 2 = 10, then adjust.
That is the exponent for one day. Multiply by 365 days: 4.5 × 10<sup>8</sup> × 3.65 × 10<sup>2</sup>.

items.hint: Write 365 in scientific notation. Multiply the fronts, add the exponents, then adjust.
items.explain:
Yearly total = (4.5 × 108) × 365 = (4.5 × 108)(3.65 × 102).

Front numbers: 4.5 × 3.65 = 16.425. Exponents: 8 + 2 = 10. So far: 16.425 × 1010.

Adjust: 16.425 = 1.6425 × 101, so the total is about 1.6 × 1011 gallons, and n = 11.

Sense check: 450 million gallons a day for about 400 days is about 180 billion, or 1.8 × 1011, close to our answer. The tempting wrong answer, 10, skips the adjustment.

items.prompt:
After a crash on dry pavement, investigators can estimate a car’s speed from its skid marks with the formula s = √(24d), where s is the speed in miles per hour and d is the length of the skid marks in feet.

The skid marks are 90 feet long. To the nearest tenth, about how fast was the car going, in miles per hour? You may use a calculator.

mistakes.why: You found 24 × 90 = 2,160 but did not take the square root. The formula is s = √(24d), so the last step is √2,160.
You took the square root of 24 only and then multiplied by 90. The root bar covers 24d, so multiply first: 24 × 90 = 2,160, then take the root.
You added 24 + 90 = 114 under the root. 24d means 24 times d: 24 × 90 = 2,160.

items.hint: The root bar groups 24d. Multiply under the root first, then take the square root, then round.
items.explain:
Substitute d = 90: s = √(24 × 90).

Grouping first (the root bar groups): 24 × 90 = 2,160, so s = √2,160.

Estimate: 462 = 2,116 and 472 = 2,209, so s is between 46 and 47. A calculator gives √2,160 ≈ 46.476.

Rounded to the nearest tenth, the car was going about 46.5 miles per hour.

The tempting wrong answer, 2,160, stops before taking the square root. Another common slip is taking the root of 24 alone (√24 × 90 ≈ 440.9), which ignores that the root bar covers the whole product.

items.prompt: Which expression has the greatest value?
why: Without parentheses the exponent touches only the 2: −2<sup>4</sup> = −(2 × 2 × 2 × 2) = −16, the least of the four.
2<sup>−4</sup> = 1/2<sup>4</sup> = 1/16. A negative exponent gives a small positive fraction, which is less than 16.
(−2)<sup>3</sup> = −8. Three negative factors, an odd number, give a negative answer.
items.hint: Evaluate each one. Find the base first, and count negative factors.
items.explain:
(−2)4 = (−2)(−2)(−2)(−2) = 16.

−24 = −16.   2−4 = 1/16.   (−2)3 = −8.

The greatest is (−2)4 = 16.

The tempting mistake is reading −24 as 16. Without parentheses, the negative sign is not part of the base.

items.prompt: Which expression is equivalent to (x4)3 · x−2?
why: You added the exponents in the power of a power (4 + 3 = 7), then 7 + (−2) = 5. A power of a power multiplies: (x<sup>4</sup>)<sup>3</sup> = x<sup>12</sup>.
You subtracted −2 instead of adding it: 12 − (−2) = 14. Multiplying powers adds the exponents: 12 + (−2) = 10.
You multiplied 12 × (−2). Multiplying powers with the same base adds the exponents: 12 + (−2) = 10.
items.hint: Do the power of a power first, then use the product rule.
items.explain:
Power of a power: (x4)3 = x4×3 = x12.

Product rule: x12 · x−2 = x12+(−2) = x10.

Plug-in check with x = 2: (24)3 · 2−2 = 4,096 × 1/4 = 1,024 = 210.

The most tempting wrong answer, x5, adds 4 + 3 inside the power of a power.

items.prompt: Evaluate 2−2 + 40. Enter a fraction or a decimal.

You treated 4<sup>0</sup> as 0. Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1, so add 1/4 + 1.
You treated 2<sup>−2</sup> as 2<sup>2</sup> = 4. The negative exponent means reciprocal: 1/4, not 4.

items.hint: A negative exponent means reciprocal. A zero exponent gives 1.
items.explain:
2−2 = 1/22 = 1/4.

40 = 1.

1/4 + 1 = 1 1/4 (1.25 or 5/4).

The tempting wrong answer, 0.25, treats the zero power as 0.

items.prompt: Evaluate √(62 + 82).

mistakes.why: You split the root across the addition: √(6<sup>2</sup>) + √(8<sup>2</sup>) = 6 + 8. The root bar groups: add first, 36 + 64 = 100, then √100 = 10.
You added under the root correctly but did not take the square root. √100 = 10.
You doubled 6 and 8 instead of squaring them (12 + 16 = 28) and did not take the root. 6<sup>2</sup> = 36 and 8<sup>2</sup> = 64.

items.hint: Everything under the root bar is grouped. Simplify it first, then take the root.
items.explain:
Under the root: 62 = 36 and 82 = 64, so 36 + 64 = 100.

√100 = 10.

The tempting wrong answer, 14, splits the root across addition. √(a + b) is not √a + √b.

items.prompt:
Choose the answers that make each statement true.

√60 is between {{0}} and {{1}}.

In simplest form, √60 = {{2}}.

8<sup>2</sup> = 64 is more than 60, so 8 is the upper number, not the lower one.

7 is the lower number. 7<sup>2</sup> = 49 is less than 60, so you need the next whole number.
9<sup>2</sup> = 81, but 8<sup>2</sup> = 64 is already more than 60. Use the closest perfect square above 60.

You put the wrong factor outside. In 60 = 4 × 15, the perfect square is 4, so 2 comes out and 15 stays inside.

items.explain:
72 = 49 and 82 = 64, and 49 < 60 < 64, so √60 is between 7 and 8.
